findings.text: System suspend entry validates the requested sleep level against the supported range and rejects out-of-range values. Accepted requests are traced through a common transition path with entry and exit diagnostics, and the resulting status is recorded in the suspend statistics before returning to the caller.

Sleep transitions progress through validation, exclusive acquisition of the system transition guard, optional idle-state reset and filesystem synchronization, preparation, an early freezer self-test exit, device suspension, and a common finish and release phase. Failure at any preparatory stage unwinds through the same finish path and releases the guard.

Preparation requires reported support for the target state, then prepares the console, notifies observers with a robust pair, freezes filesystems, and freezes tasks with tracing. If task freezing fails the failure step is recorded and filesystems, observers and console are restored in reverse order; the normal finish path thaws tasks and filesystems and restores observers and console.

Task freezing is available in two build variants. The active variant freezes user tasks first and then kernel threads, thawing user tasks if the second phase fails, while the alternate variant always reports success without action. Thawing similarly has an active variant that thaws tasks and a no-operation variant that does nothing.

Suspend outcome accounting maintains monotonic success and failure totals. Failures append the error code and the failed step into fixed-size circular histories with independent wrap-around positions, preserving only the most recent entries.

Hibernation output to swap follows an acquire, incremental write, finalize and release lifecycle. Acquisition validates the resume target and secures a map page plus an initial location. Incremental writes chain additional map pages as needed. Finalization records the image header, persists the last map page, and on any error discards all allocated swap locations before releasing resources and closing the device.

The writer tracks a low-memory watermark equal to one half of currently observed free low memory. The value is captured during setup, refreshed after large threaded allocations, and recomputed whenever throttling waits for in-flight writes, ensuring write-ahead never consumes more than half of free memory.

Allocated swap offsets are tracked in an ordered tree of disjoint closed intervals. Insertion merges an offset that is exactly adjacent to a neighboring interval, rejects an offset already covered as invalid, reports allocation failure distinctly, and otherwise inserts a new single-offset interval and rebalances.

Swap block acquisition translates a hibernation slot into a device location only after successful extent tracking. Tracking failure releases the slot, and any failure including missing slots yields a zero sentinel rather than a valid location.

Before saving, the writer resolves the resume target by preferring an explicitly configured device with its block offset when present, otherwise selecting the first available swap target. The chosen device is opened for writing and retained for the duration of the save; resolution or open failure aborts setup.

Individual page output distinguishes batched and unbatched contexts. Without a batch the page is written synchronously. With a batch the implementation attempts to stage through temporary storage for asynchronous submission, waiting for completions and retrying once when storage is scarce, and falling back to synchronous output with a one-time warning if staging remains unavailable. A zero destination is always rejected as out of space.

Map pages accumulate device locations until full. Overflow handling secures the next location first, links it from the current page, persists the full page, clears reuse state and resets the fill count, which avoids emitting an empty trailing map when the image size aligns exactly. When free memory reaches the watermark, pending writes are drained before continuing.

Image finalization reads the resume area and requires one of two legacy swap markers. On match it preserves the original marker, installs the hibernation marker, records the first image location and supplied flags, optionally captures hardware identity with its flag, and stores the checksum when checksum mode is requested before writing the header back. Absence of a legacy marker is reported as a missing device.

Resume probing opens the configured device for reading, clears a scratch header, and reads the resume block. A present hibernation marker triggers restoration of the preserved original marker, caching of header flags, and an immediate rewrite to reset the on-disk signature. Hardware identity mismatch or a missing marker aborts resume, with distinct diagnostics for absent images versus mismatched hardware.

Uncompressed saving initializes an asynchronous batch, iterates the snapshot until exhaustion or error, writes each page through the map writer, emits progress at decile intervals, then waits for completions, closes the batch, reports throughput, and propagates the first encountered failure including deferred completion errors.

Compressed saving bounds its worker count by online processors and a configured ceiling, requires successful staging and worker bring-up before producing output, validates each compressed result as non-empty and within worst-case size, prefixes stored output with its length so trailing padding can be discarded on read, overlaps checksum computation with compression, and guarantees worker shutdown and release of all staging on both success and failure.

Pre-save capacity checks require strictly more free swap pages than the sum of the image size plus a reserved allowance for input-output operations, with the observed free count emitted for diagnostics.

Frame packing fills a caller buffer sized to hold a page worth of machine words by repeatedly drawing the next frame from an allocation map. Encountering the end-of-map sentinel stops the fill early, and frames marked in a companion zero map have a dedicated flag bit set in the stored value.

Sleep entry acquires the system transition guard with a non-blocking attempt and treats contention as busy without waiting. Successful acquisition holds the guard across preparation, device suspension and finish, with a single release on all exit paths.

Autosleep state is guarded by a dedicated mutex. A helper offers interruptible acquisition for external coordination and a paired helper releases. State updates hold the guard while storing the new level, bracketed by hold-awake assertions that prevent concurrent sleep decisions.

Autosleep control exposes query of the current level, interruptible lock and unlock helpers, an update operation that validates against the maximum when hibernation is unavailable, enables or disables wakeup-source autosleep handling and queues suspend work when entering an active level, and a one-time initializer that registers a wakeup source and an ordered workqueue with cleanup on partial failure.
Registry nodes contain intrusive linkage under head, an associated device pointer under dev, and a requirement flag under required.

A dedicated mutex serializes all traversals and mutations of the virtual-terminal switch requirement list. Both registration/update and removal hold the mutex across search and any insertion or deletion, releasing on all paths including allocation failure and already-registered updates.

Registration looks up the device first and, if already present, only updates its requirement flag; otherwise it allocates a node, records device and requirement, and links it, reporting allocation failure distinctly. Removal unlinks and frees the matching node if present and otherwise leaves the list unchanged.

Suspend preserves the original foreground console index and kernel message verbosity in dedicated statics, alongside a completion flag recording whether the terminal switch was performed. A selector designates which console serves suspend output.
Suspend output targets the final console index, defined as one less than the maximum console count.
Messages from the energy model component share a fixed human-readable subsystem tag prepended to each log format.

Resource and state failures abort without advancing: missing map state or destinations, exhausted swap, failed allocations, absent swap markers, missing resume images, hardware mismatches, out-of-range or unsupported sleep levels, contended transitions, failed filesystem synchronization, and failed preparation all return errors, with swap paths discarding partial allocations and suspend paths unwinding through common finish and release.

The defining fragments use external linkage for hibernation swap allocation and resume validation, system suspend entry and its outcome and step accounting, autosleep query and control with initialization, and virtual-terminal switch registration and removal, making them callable from other compilation units in the build.
